text: The t-test compares averages of numbers. But much of business data is categorical — a customer bought or didn't, a ticket was about billing, shipping, or login. To test claims about counts in categories you use a chi-square test, written with the Greek letter chi squared. It answers questions like: is the mix of categories different from what I'd expect by chance?

Take a table of counts. Under the null hypothesis, you can work out how many observations you'd expect in each cell. The chi-square statistic adds up how far the observed counts are from those expected counts, squared and divided by expected. If observed is close to expected, the statistic is small; if it diverges, it's large, and under the null it follows a chi-square distribution whose shape depends on degrees of freedom.

A support team gets 300 tickets in a week, spread across five weekdays as 70, 55, 50, 58, and 67. Is the workload evenly distributed, with 60 expected per day? scipy's chisquare gives a statistic of 4.633 and p equals 0.327 — the day-to-day variation is entirely plausible under an even workload. That's not proof the load is perfectly even — with only 300 tickets, moderate imbalances could still hide.

The more common case: did the purchase rate differ by device? Across 2,000 sessions split among mobile, desktop, and tablet, chi2_contingency gives a statistic of 12.483, p equals 0.0019, with 2 degrees of freedom. The null hypothesis is that purchase and device are independent — the purchase rate is the same for every device. With p this small, independence looks implausible.

A significant chi-square only says somewhere there's a difference, not where. Looking at the actual rates: 12.0 percent for mobile, 13.6 percent for desktop, 20.0 percent for tablet. The expected tablet purchases were 41.2 but we observed 60 — tablets clearly drive this result, while mobile and desktop stay close to each other.

Standardized residuals confirm it — observed minus expected, over the square root of expected — the tablet bought cell comes out around 2.9, far larger than any other cell. As always, significance isn't magnitude. Cramér's V scales chi-square to a 0 to 1 range, and here it comes out to about 0.079 — a small association. There's a real difference, but device explains only a little of who actually buys.

A few assumptions and cautions. Counts must be counts of independent observations, not percentages or repeated measurements of the same customers. Expected counts shouldn't be too small — a common guideline is at least 5 in most cells, and for small 2 by 2 tables, use Fisher's exact test instead.

Chi-square finds association, not causation — tablet users might differ from mobile users in plenty of other ways too. And large samples make trivial associations significant, so always check Cramér's V alongside the p-value. To recap: chi-square compares observed counts to expected counts under the null. Goodness-of-fit checks one variable; the test of independence checks two. Follow a significant result with cell-level inspection and an effect size. Next: comparing three or more group means with ANOVA.
